items.title: Pete Candoli interviewed by Monk Rowe, Los Angeles, California, February 15, 1999
items.q: Sweets was there, Sweets, Harry Edison, my dear friend. We do a lot of the Blue Note things with Lionel Hampton and the Golden Men of Music

ctx.x: So how did — did you eventually decide, let’s see, late 40s, early 50s, that the road thing was getting a little old?

No it wasn’t getting too old, not really. But I was into, I remember like in ’43 I think it was Tommy Dorsey’s band or ’42 or sometime, I took Ziggy’s place and I remember playing lead on an all-star Metronome date. And Sweets was there, Sweets, Harry Edison, my dear friend. We do a lot of the Blue Note things with Lionel Hampton and the Golden Men of Music, you know that. And I found an old album, and I don’t have any albums, this must have been really in storage. Tommy Dorsey was playing lead trombone, I was…

items.title: 68427_Harry Edison oral history interview
items.q: I can attribute to those guys, the conversation and the experience that I had playing with them

ctx.x: Ray Linn was out here at the time. He was in the studio bands. Those guys were trained musicians, you know. They had been taking lessons on their horns when

my mother couldn't even afford to give me lessons, you know. But they were trained to do that and I owe a lot of my success in the studios -- I can attribute to those guys, the conversation and the experience that I had playing with them, and their knowledge that they gave me that was -- I think, my success in the studios was due to them. Because I knew --
They could tell you technical things.
